title: Records, Dataclasses and Equality
oneLiner: C# records and Python dataclasses, copies with with and replace, value equality versus identity, Equals and GetHashCode versus __eq__ and __hash__, why changeable keys break sets and dictionaries, and ordering your own types.
keyTakeaway: Records and dataclasses generate a constructor, readable printing and value equality from the field list. Sets and dictionaries use a hash code and then equality, so equal objects must hash equally: override both together, and only use objects that can't change (records, frozen dataclasses, strings, tuples) as keys.
explanation:
Many classes exist mainly to hold data: a reading, an order line, a point. Writing their constructors, printing and comparison by hand is repetitive and easy to get subtly wrong, so C# has record types and Python has dataclasses, which generate all of it from a list of fields.

The most important thing they generate is value equality: two objects with the same data are equal, the way two strings with the same text are. Ordinary classes compare by identity instead, asking whether both sides are the same object. Neither is wrong; they suit different things.

Equality matters most inside hash sets and dictionaries. These find a key by first computing its hash code, a number derived from the key that says which bucket to look in, and then checking equality within that bucket. So objects that are equal must produce the same hash code, and a key must not change while it's stored, or it will be looked for in the wrong bucket. The lesson shows both failures and how records, frozen dataclasses and a hand-written Equals and GetHashCode (or __eq__ and __hash__) avoid them. It ends with ordering: making your own types sortable with IComparable<T> or order=True.
